title: Should You Allow Your Students To Talk During Independent Work?
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Answering readers' most-requested question of the year, Linsin argues unequivocally against allowing student talk during independent work. He contends that even quiet chatter cuts through concentration instantly because the brain reflexively tries to decipher speech, and that repeated interruptions prevent students from ever reaching the productive mental state of flow. Beyond immediate focus, he argues that permitting talk erodes the broader 'muscle' of independence, producing a class that can't sustain attention, struggles academically, and depends on constant external stimulation — while silence, by contrast, builds a resilience that even helps students with attention difficulties. His answer to logistical worries like questions or borrowed supplies is to front-load preparation so students can work entirely without help, calling full independence 'the summit of the mountain of good teaching.'
points: Even whispered talking breaks concentration instantly because the brain reflexively tries to decipher what's being said.
Repeated interruptions prevent students from reaching a productive state of flow, turning independent work into a dreaded slog.
Independence is described as a muscle built through daily practice, and allowing talk weakens it for every student in the room, not just the talkers.
Unrestricted talk during independent work is linked to weaker writing ability, memory, listening skills, and overall academic progress.
Logistical needs — questions, help, borrowed supplies — should be solved through upfront preparation, not by permitting conversation during work time.
quotes: Independent practice is the most critical factor in developing academic skill and competency.
But talking, even whispering? Like a surprised knock on your front door, it cuts straight through to the prefrontal cortex, breaking concentration in an instant.
It takes several minutes of quiet focus to get into a state of flow , whereby time slips by unnoticed, performance soars, and the very act of doing the work becomes an enjoyable experience.

Independence is a muscle students develop through daily practice. It results in an ability – a superpower in this day and age of shortening attention spans – they can enjoy and carry with them into the future.
One thing is for sure, if you do allow talking, then the ability to attend will weaken for all students. You’ll create a dependent, immature class that can’t sit still for more than ten minutes.
You take care of all of this beforehand by preparing your students to succeed all on their own—yes, every student—and without help from you, their classmates, or anyone else.
